Additional usage of statomatic

Source: vignettes/additional_workflows.Rmd
additional_workflows.Rmd

This vignette demonstrates additional usage of the statomatic package beyond that shown in the basic workflow vignette. It is recommended to read the basic workflow vignette before reading this one.

Begin by loading the statomatic package 

library(statomatic)

A general overview

multigroup_main() and twogroup_main() run the whole statomatic analysis. Each of their steps is also available as a separate function, which can be used on its own. This section shows how.

We’ll use the same normalized counts that were used in the multi-group, two-factor example of the basic workflow vignette.

x <- read.csv("normalized_counts.csv")
x <- cf(x)
head(x)
#>                    Sample_600 Sample_601 Sample_602 Sample_616 Sample_617

As before, cf() moves the gene ids from the first column into the row names, so the data.frame contains only the numbers we want to analyze. Reading the file with read.csv("normalized_counts.csv", row.names = 1) does the same.

We also need a sample_info data.frame that maps our samples (the columns of x) to the experimental factors.

sample_info <- data.frame(sample = colnames(x),
                          sex = c(rep("Male", 10), rep("Female", 10)),
                          genotype = c(rep("WT", 5), rep("KO", 5), rep("WT", 5), rep("KO", 5)))
sample_info
#>        sample    sex genotype
#> 1  Sample_600   Male       WT
#> 2  Sample_601   Male       WT
#> 3  Sample_602   Male       WT
#> 4  Sample_616   Male       WT
#> 5  Sample_617   Male       WT
#> 6  Sample_603   Male       KO
#> 7  Sample_604   Male       KO
#> 8  Sample_605   Male       KO
#> 9  Sample_606   Male       KO
#> 10 Sample_621   Male       KO
#> 11 Sample_607 Female       WT
#> 12 Sample_608 Female       WT
#> 13 Sample_609 Female       WT
#> 14 Sample_610 Female       WT
#> 15 Sample_623 Female       WT
#> 16 Sample_611 Female       KO
#> 17 Sample_612 Female       KO
#> 18 Sample_613 Female       KO
#> 19 Sample_614 Female       KO
#> 20 Sample_615 Female       KO

The steps inside multigroup_main

multigroup_main(x, sample_info, factors = c("sex", "genotype")) does the following:

  1. Matches the rows of sample_info to the columns of x by sample name, checks the design, and combines the factors into groups (Female_KO, Female_WT, Male_KO and Male_WT).
  2. Sorts the rows of x into the ne, nu and nn sets with test_norm().
  3. Calculates fold changes between every pair of groups with fold_change().
  4. Tests each set:
    • ne: run_anova() with all factors, then run_tukey() on the groups
    • nu: run_welch() and run_dunnett() on the groups
    • nn: run_kruskal() and run_dunn() on the groups
  5. Combines each set’s results with the fold changes.

twogroup_main() follows the same steps, with run_ttest(), run_welch() and run_wilcox().

Using the functions individually

There is one important difference between the main functions and the individual functions. The main functions match samples to their groups by name. The individual functions don’t: they take the group labels as a plain vector, and the labels must be in the same order as the columns of x. If they are not, the results will be wrong without any error.

A safe way to get the labels in the right order is to look them up by sample name:

idx <- match(colnames(x), sample_info$sample)
sex <- sample_info$sex[idx]
genotype <- sample_info$genotype[idx]

For the pairwise tests and fold changes, the groups are the combinations of the factors, joined with “_“, as multigroup_main() does:

group <- paste(sex, genotype, sep = "_")
group
#>  [1] "Male_WT"   "Male_WT"   "Male_WT"   "Male_WT"   "Male_WT"   "Male_KO"  
#>  [7] "Male_KO"   "Male_KO"   "Male_KO"   "Male_KO"   "Female_WT" "Female_WT"
#> [13] "Female_WT" "Female_WT" "Female_WT" "Female_KO" "Female_KO" "Female_KO"
#> [19] "Female_KO" "Female_KO"

test_norm() sorts the rows of the data by the distribution of their residuals and the equality of variances between groups. With two or more factors, give it a data.frame with one column per factor:

sorted <- test_norm(x, data.frame(sex = sex, genotype = genotype))
names(sorted)
#> [1] "ne"    "nu"    "nn"    "tests"

The result is a list. ne has the rows with normally distributed residuals and equal variances, nu the rows with normally distributed residuals but unequal variances, and nn the rows with residuals that are not normally distributed. tests shows the Shapiro-Wilk and Levene p-values of every row and the set it was sorted into:

head(sorted$tests)
#>                         shapiro    levene set
#> ENSMUSG00000051285 5.955714e-01 0.4443846  ne
#> ENSMUSG00000057363 3.464768e-01 0.2722540  ne
#> ENSMUSG00000100555 3.976942e-05 0.6284235  nn
#> ENSMUSG00000078184 7.456867e-01 0.5382225  ne
#> ENSMUSG00000061024 3.367137e-01 0.7158967  ne
#> ENSMUSG00000025911 9.854698e-02 0.7137068  ne

To use test_norm() with only one factor, give it a vector instead:

sorted_one_factor <- test_norm(x, group)
table(sorted_one_factor$tests$set)
#> 
#> ne nu nn 
#> 62  1 37

The usage of the rest of the functions is similar, and their names describe what they do: run_anova() runs an ANOVA, run_tukey() runs a Tukey test, and so on.

run_anova() takes one factor (a vector) or several (a data.frame), and runs a one-way, two-way or three-way ANOVA accordingly. It uses Type II sums of squares, so the order of the factors doesn’t change the results.

anova_res <- run_anova(sorted$ne, data.frame(sex = sex, genotype = genotype))
head(anova_res)
#>                    pvalue_sex  padj_sex pvalue_genotype padj_genotype
#> ENSMUSG00000051285  0.4181785 0.9384844       0.4267951     0.7520794
#> ENSMUSG00000057363  0.6363190 0.9866797       0.3757298     0.7059165
#> ENSMUSG00000078184  0.3813036 0.9384844       0.9576038     0.9895239
#> ENSMUSG00000061024  0.1879463 0.9384844       0.5524404     0.7611401
#> ENSMUSG00000025911  0.5146527 0.9384844       0.3078191     0.6998790
#> ENSMUSG00000057335  0.9928111 0.9935637       0.1615905     0.5288119
#>                    pvalue_sex:genotype padj_sex:genotype
#> ENSMUSG00000051285          0.79596064         0.9913574
#> ENSMUSG00000057363          0.70346317         0.9913574
#> ENSMUSG00000078184          0.57458343         0.9913574
#> ENSMUSG00000061024          0.08030823         0.9913574
#> ENSMUSG00000025911          0.83172345         0.9913574
#> ENSMUSG00000057335          0.85432131         0.9913574

The other test functions take a single grouping: run_tukey(), run_welch(), run_dunnett(), run_kruskal() and run_dunn() for more than two groups, and run_ttest(), run_welch() and run_wilcox() for two groups.

tukey_res <- run_tukey(sorted$ne, group)
head(tukey_res)

fold_change() calculates the log2 fold change between every pair of groups, and the mean of each group:

fc <- fold_change(x, group)

If the data is already log-transformed, use fold_change(x, group, log_input = TRUE). The fold change is then the difference between the group means. The main functions have the same log_input argument.

Data in a SummarizedExperiment

If your data is stored in a SummarizedExperiment (for example from Bioconductor), pass its assay and its sample information to the main functions:

library(SummarizedExperiment)
res <- multigroup_main(assay(se), as.data.frame(colData(se)), factors = c("sex", "genotype"))

A more advanced example

In this example we have six different tables we want to analyze. These tables are from a metagenomic analysis, and contain abundance information at the phylum, class, order, family, genus and species level. We looked at the species data before, in the basic workflow vignette.

There are 24 samples in this experiment in 3 groups, with 8 samples per group. We’ll call the groups group1, group2 and group3, and analyze them with multigroup_main() with one factor.

We’re going to apply the statomatic method to all six tables, to identify differences between groups at each taxonomic level.

We read in the data all together and store it in a list.

# get all files in the current directory with abundance.csv in the name
a <- list.files(".", pattern = "abundance.csv")
a
#> [1] "class_abundance.csv"   "family_abundance.csv"  "genus_abundance.csv"  
#> [4] "order_abundance.csv"   "phylum_abundance.csv"  "species_abundance.csv"

Notice that the file names are in alphabetical order.

# read them in with read.csv
read_in <- lapply(a, read.csv)
# look at the first three rows of each table
lapply(read_in, head, 3)

Each of these tables needs the cf function.

# apply cf to each table
tables <- lapply(read_in, cf)

We can use the same sample_info for all of these tables, since they all contain the same samples.

# tables[[1]] is the first table in the tables list. all the tables have the same column names
sample_info <- data.frame(sample = colnames(tables[[1]]),
                          group = c(rep("group1", 8), rep("group2", 8), rep("group3", 8)))
sample_info
#>       sample  group
#> 1   sample_1 group1
#> 2   sample_2 group1
#> 3   sample_3 group1
#> 4   sample_4 group1
#> 5   sample_5 group1
#> 6   sample_6 group1
#> 7   sample_7 group1
#> 8   sample_8 group1
#> 9   sample_9 group2
#> 10 sample_10 group2
#> 11 sample_11 group2
#> 12 sample_12 group2
#> 13 sample_13 group2
#> 14 sample_14 group2
#> 15 sample_15 group2
#> 16 sample_16 group2
#> 17 sample_17 group3
#> 18 sample_18 group3
#> 19 sample_19 group3
#> 20 sample_20 group3
#> 21 sample_21 group3
#> 22 sample_22 group3
#> 23 sample_23 group3
#> 24 sample_24 group3

Now we’ll apply the multigroup_main function to each of these tables, again using lapply. verbose = FALSE turns off the progress messages, which would otherwise be printed for every table, and set.seed() makes the Dunnett T3 p-values reproducible.

set.seed(1)
res <- lapply(tables, multigroup_main, sample_info = sample_info, factors = "group", verbose = FALSE)

We know from before that multigroup_main returns a list, and we just applied this function to a list of data.frames. So what is res? It’s a list of lists.

# res has 6 elements, one per table we analyzed
length(res)
#> [1] 6
# each element of res has 8 elements
length(res[[1]])
#> [1] 8
names(res[[1]])
#> [1] "anova_results" "welch_results" "kw_results"    "foldchanges"  
#> [5] "ne"            "nu"            "nn"            "tests"

Each element of res is the same as it was when we were only analyzing one table. The only difference is that now we’re working with several of them at once.

We’ll look at the results of the first one just to orient ourselves, and we’re only going to look at the first three elements: the ANOVA, Welch and Kruskal-Wallis results.

# get the first element of res (a list of the results of the first analysis).
# This is the class abundances, since it is first alphabetically
x <- res[[1]]
lapply(x[1:3], head)

With one factor, the results of all three sets have the same columns, so we can combine each table’s results into a single data.frame.

For each list of results in res, we’ll rbind (row bind) the first three elements, save this combined table to a new list and then give it a name.

For the names, we’ll use the result of the list.files function above, but we’ll remove the .csv extension first.

# remove .csv from the file names
name_list <- sub("\\.csv$", "", a)
name_list
#> [1] "class_abundance"   "family_abundance"  "genus_abundance"  
#> [4] "order_abundance"   "phylum_abundance"  "species_abundance"

Now we’ll combine and save the tables.

# define an empty list for our new tables
collated_tables <- list()
# use a for loop to combine and save our tables
for (i in seq_along(res)) {
  # the current result we're processing
  temp <- res[[i]]
  # get just the p-values and fold change results
  first_three <- temp[1:3]
  # rbind into one new table
  new_table <- rbind(first_three[[1]], first_three[[2]], first_three[[3]])
  # save the new table to the collated_tables list
  collated_tables[[i]] <- new_table
}
# set the names of collated_tables to be the names from name_list
names(collated_tables) <- name_list
# look at some of the results
lapply(collated_tables, head, 3)

From here, we could do some further analysis or filtering of the results. One way to export them is to write.csv each of the elements of collated_tables, with the same file name as the original abundance table, with results_ at the beginning.

for (i in seq_along(collated_tables)) {
  write.csv(collated_tables[[i]], paste0("results_", a[i]))
}
